questions.question: Explain, using the neutral axis, why a steel ruler on edge carries far more than the same ruler laid flat, and why material near the middle of a beam can be removed to save mass.
questions.expected_answer: In bending, the fibres furthest from the neutral axis are stretched or compressed most and carry most of the load, while material near the axis is almost idle. Standing the ruler on edge increases the section's depth in the direction of bending, placing its material far from the neutral axis where it works; the same mass is then about four times as stiff and twice as strong for a doubling of depth, whereas doubling width only doubles both. Because material near the neutral axis contributes little, it can be thinned to a web and the material concentrated into flanges at top and bottom, keeping most of the bending strength at a fraction of the mass, which is the I-beam and also the logic of tubes and corrugated sheet.

questions.question: Describe the I-beam, angle iron and T-bar: the parts of each, the force each carries best, where each is used, and one weakness of each.
questions.expected_answer: I-beam: a vertical web joining two horizontal flanges; the flanges carry tension and compression in bending about the strong axis and the web carries shear; used for floor beams, girders, crane rails and lintels; weak in bending about the other axis and in torsion, so long beams are braced. Angle iron (L): two legs at right angles; stiff in two directions and easy to bolt or weld in corners; used for frames, gates, brackets, truss bracing and tank-stand legs; a single angle twists and bends unevenly under heavy load, so they are often paired. T-bar: one flange and a stem, behaving like half an I-beam; used where one face must be flat, as lintels, stiffeners and rails, and mirrored by the concrete T-beam; weaker than an I-beam because it has only one flange.

questions.question: Set out the three steps for selecting a section, match each type of force to its best section, and explain how shaped sections save material and reduce environmental impact.
questions.expected_answer: Steps: name the main force on the member; match the section to it; check connections and practical constraints such as bolting or welding, space, stock sizes and the need for a flat face. Matching: bending about one axis wants depth, so an I-beam or T-bar; compression wants material far from the centre in all directions to resist buckling, so a tube or paired angles; torsion wants a closed tube; pure tension needs only sufficient area, so flat or round bar. Shaped sections concentrate material where the force acts, so a member carries the same load at a fraction of the mass of a solid bar; since steel is sold by mass and its production consumes energy and emits carbon dioxide, less steel means less mining, smelting, transport, foundation concrete and scrap, which reduces the structure's negative impact.
